description: The enduring ideas from the canonical software engineering books and papers (Brooks, Parnas, Ousterhout, Fowler, GoF, Feathers, SICP, Bentley, Unix, Peopleware, Accelerate, Nygard, Kent, Norman and the classic papers), organised by idea rather than by book. For an architect who wants the arguments behind the slogans.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: How does Ousterhout define complexity in software?
notes.back: Anything in the structure of a system that makes it hard to understand and modify. Judged by the reader, not the writer.
notes.extra: Test: if other people find it complex, it is complex, whatever the author thinks.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Why does Ousterhout insist on a zero-tolerance stance toward complexity?
notes.back: Complexity is incremental: it arrives in small, individually reasonable doses. No single dose is worth refusing, so only a blanket refusal works.
notes.analogy: Death by a thousand cuts: no cut is fatal, so you must refuse the first one.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.text: Ousterhout's three symptoms of complexity: {{c1::change amplification}} (a small change touches many places), {{c2::cognitive load}} (how much you must know to make a change), {{c3::unknown unknowns}} (it is not obvious which code must change).
notes.analogy: Fixing a typo in the mail-merge template (one place) vs correcting the same address in 200 printed letters.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Why are unknown unknowns the worst of Ousterhout's three symptoms?
notes.back: With the other two you at least know what to learn or touch. Here you cannot tell that you are missing something until it breaks.
notes.analogy: A map with a missing road is worse than a long route: you don't know you're lost.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.text: Ousterhout's two root causes of complexity: {{c1::dependencies}} (code cannot be understood or changed in isolation) and {{c2::obscurity}} (important information is not obvious). Every design technique in the book reduces one of them.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Essential vs accidental complexity (Brooks): how to tell them apart?
notes.back: Essential: inherent in the problem, survives any tooling. Accidental: created by our languages, tools and representations, and removable.
notes.analogy: A surgeon's essential difficulty is the body; a dull scalpel is accidental.
notes.extra: Test: would a perfect language and infinite machine make it go away? If yes, it was accidental.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.text: Brooks' four essential difficulties of software: {{c1::complexity}} (no two parts alike; states explode), {{c2::conformity}} (must fit arbitrary human institutions), {{c3::changeability}} (software is pressured to change because it can), {{c4::invisibility}} (no geometric representation to reason with).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Why does Brooks conclude there is no silver bullet?
notes.back: Past 10× gains (high-level languages, time-sharing, integrated development environments (IDEs)) removed accidental difficulty. What remains is mostly essential, so no single technique can give another order of magnitude.
notes.extra: Framing: the claim is about a single development within a decade; it does not say progress is impossible.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.text: Brooks' promising attacks on essential complexity: {{c1::buy rather than build}}, {{c2::refine requirements with rapid prototyping}}, {{c3::grow software incrementally rather than build it}}, {{c4::find and nurture great designers}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Brooks' tar pit: why does a working program cost ~9× more as a product you can ship?
notes.back: ×3 to make it a product (generalised, tested, documented) and ×3 to make it a system (integrated with defined interfaces). Both multiply.
notes.analogy: A prototype in the garage vs a car that passes crash tests and fits a parts catalogue.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Out of the Tar Pit: what are the two main sources of complexity?
notes.back: State and control (the order in which things happen). Both are mostly accidental, pushed on us by our languages.
notes.source: Moseley & Marks · Out of the Tar Pit

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Why does Out of the Tar Pit rank mutable state as the worst enemy?
notes.back: Each state variable multiplies the cases to test and reason about, and one component's state contaminates its callers, so you cannot reason locally.
notes.analogy: A light switch with memory: the same press does different things depending on history you can't see.
notes.source: Moseley & Marks · Out of the Tar Pit

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Out of the Tar Pit: what is accidental state, and what should happen to it?
notes.back: State that can be derived from essential (user-supplied) state, e.g. caches and denormalised copies. Derive it; never maintain it by hand.
notes.extra: Ideal proposed: functional relational programming — essential state as relations, logic as pure functions.
notes.source: Moseley & Marks · Out of the Tar Pit

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: McConnell's Primary Technical Imperative?
notes.back: Managing complexity: minimise the essential complexity any one person must hold at a time, and stop accidental complexity from proliferating.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::01 Complexity & Its Sources
notes.front: Hickey's simple vs easy: what is the difference?
notes.back: Simple = one braid, not interleaved with other things (objective). Easy = near at hand, familiar (relative to you). Easy things are often complected.
notes.analogy: A single thread vs a knotted braid: the braid is handy to grab but impossible to pull apart.
notes.extra: Verb: to complect = to braid together. Hickey's examples: state complects value and time; inheritance complects types.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Parnas' criterion for decomposing a system into modules?
notes.back: Cut around design decisions likely to change, each hidden inside one module, not around steps in the processing flowchart.
notes.analogy: Pack a suitcase by what you'll unpack together, not by the order you bought things.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: What did Parnas' key word in context (KWIC) index example show?
notes.back: The same program decomposed by processing steps or by hidden decisions. Only the second survives a change of line-storage format without touching every module.
notes.extra: Modules in the second version: line storage, circular shifter, alphabetiser, input/output, master control. Each owns one secret.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Information hiding vs encapsulation: how do they differ?
notes.back: Encapsulation is the language mechanism (bundling, access control). Information hiding is the design decision about which secrets the interface conceals. You can encapsulate yet hide nothing.
notes.extra: Example: a class with private fields and a getter/setter for each is encapsulated but leaks every decision.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Deep vs shallow module: how to tell?
notes.back: Deep: small interface, lots of functionality behind it. Shallow: interface nearly as complex as the implementation, so it hides little.
notes.analogy: A vending machine is deep: one button, a whole supply chain behind it.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Ousterhout's canonical deep module example?
notes.back: Unix file input/output (I/O): open/read/write/lseek/close hide caching, drivers, permissions and block allocation behind five calls.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: What is classitis, and what does it produce?
notes.back: The belief that smaller classes are always better. It produces many shallow classes whose interfaces together outweigh the functionality.
notes.analogy: Flat-pack furniture where every bracket is sold separately and you must assemble the shelf before using it.
notes.extra: Example: Java needs FileInputStream + BufferedInputStream + ObjectInputStream to read objects with buffering; buffering should be the default.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: What is information leakage?
notes.back: A design decision reflected in more than one module (e.g. two classes both know a file format). Changing it means changing them together.
notes.analogy: Two departments each keeping their own copy of the price list: change one and the other is silently stale.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Why is back-door leakage worse than leakage through an interface?
notes.back: Shared assumptions that appear nowhere in any signature can't be seen from the interface. A reader has no way to know the modules are coupled.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Temporal decomposition: what is the red flag?
notes.back: Splitting modules by when things happen (read, modify, write). Knowledge needed at several times, like the file format, ends up duplicated.
notes.analogy: Organising a kitchen by meal (breakfast cupboard, dinner cupboard) puts the salt in three places.
notes.extra: Fix: decompose around knowledge, not around the order of execution.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Ousterhout's advice to make modules 'somewhat general-purpose'?
notes.back: Implement today's needs, but with an interface general enough for several uses. A smaller, more general interface is deeper.
notes.extra: Example: text editor insert(pos, text) / delete(start, end) instead of backspace(), deleteSelection().

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Pull complexity downward: what does it ask of a module author?
notes.back: Take the hard parts into the implementation so the interface stays simple. A module's developers should suffer so its many users don't.
notes.analogy: A good hotel concierge absorbs the hassle so guests never see it.
notes.extra: Smell: exposing a configuration parameter often pushes a decision up to users who know less than you.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Define errors out of existence: what does it mean?
notes.back: Change the semantics so the exceptional case is normal behaviour, removing the error path altogether.
notes.analogy: Asking someone to open a door that is already open: the request simply succeeds.
notes.extra: Examples: Tcl unset of a missing variable succeeds (goal already met); clamping substring ranges instead of throwing.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Why does Ousterhout treat exceptions as a leading source of complexity?
notes.back: Each exception adds a rarely exercised path that callers must handle, and handling code is itself error-prone. Fewer exceptional cases, less complexity.
notes.extra: Other tools: mask exceptions low down (TCP retransmits), aggregate handlers, or just crash for the truly rare.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Design it twice: why bother with a second design?
notes.back: Your first idea is rarely best. Two radically different designs compared on interface simplicity and generality either yield a better one or explain why the first was right.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: What is an abstraction barrier in Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)?
notes.back: A layer of constructors and selectors separating how data is used from how it is represented. Code above the barrier never touches the representation.
notes.analogy: A restaurant menu: diners order dishes; how the kitchen stores ingredients is invisible.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.text: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP): every powerful language supplies {{c1::primitive expressions}}, {{c2::means of combination}} and {{c3::means of abstraction}}. Judge an API or domain-specific language (DSL) by the same three.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Lampson's 'don't hide power' vs Parnas' 'hide secrets': how do they coexist?
notes.back: Hide decisions (representation, algorithm) but not capability: a low-level abstraction should not cost clients the performance the layer below offers.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::02 Modules, Abstraction & Information Hiding
notes.front: Parnas' 'uses' hierarchy: what does it buy you?
notes.back: If A is correct only when B is present, A uses B. Keep that relation loop-free and you can ship subsets and extensions of one program family.
notes.extra: The clean theory behind layering and later the Dependency Rule.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)'s preface claim about who programs are for?
notes.back: Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Kernighan's argument against clever code?
notes.back: Debugging is twice as hard as writing. Write code as cleverly as you can and you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it.
notes.source: Kernighan & Plauger · Elements of Programming Style

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.text: Kernighan & Plauger maxims: {{c1::write clearly, don't be too clever}}; {{c2::choose a data representation that makes the program simple}}; {{c3::don't patch bad code, rewrite it}}; {{c4::test programs at their boundary values}}; don't stop with your first draft.
notes.source: Kernighan & Plauger · Elements of Programming Style

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.text: Ousterhout's four excuses for not commenting, all rejected: {{c1::good code is self-documenting}}, {{c2::no time}}, {{c3::comments get out of date}}, {{c4::the comments I've seen are worthless}}.
notes.extra: Rebuttal in one line: code cannot express intent, rationale, units, invariants or the abstraction; that is what comments are for.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: What should a comment say, according to Ousterhout?
notes.back: What is not obvious from the code, at a different level of precision: lower (units, null semantics, boundaries) or higher (intent, abstraction).
notes.extra: Red flag: Comment Repeats Code.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Interface comment vs implementation comment: what does each carry?
notes.back: Interface: the abstraction, what the module does and its contract, nothing about how. Implementation: why the code is the way it is.
notes.extra: Red flag: Implementation Documentation Contaminates Interface.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Why does Ousterhout say to write the comments first?
notes.back: The interface comment is a design test: if the abstraction is hard to describe or the comment is long, the abstraction is bad. Fix it before coding.
notes.analogy: The comment is the canary in the coal mine of design.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Clean Code's 'comments are always failures': what is the standard objection?
notes.back: Comments carry what code cannot: intent, rationale, units, invariants. Ousterhout, McConnell and Kernighan all treat them as design tools, not failures.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.text: Clean Code naming rules: names should be {{c1::intention-revealing}}, avoid {{c2::disinformation}} (accountList that isn't a list), make {{c3::meaningful distinctions}} (no a1, a2, no noise words like Info), be {{c4::pronounceable and searchable}}; one word per concept.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Ousterhout: what does it mean when a good name is hard to find?
notes.back: The underlying design is probably unclear: the variable or method does more than one thing or has no clean abstraction. Fix the design, not the thesaurus.
notes.extra: War story: a block variable holding both logical and physical block numbers hid a bug for months.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: The main criticism of 'functions should be tiny'?
notes.back: Behaviour gets smeared across many fragments that must be read together (Ousterhout's conjoined methods). Split only when it creates a deeper abstraction.
notes.extra: Data point: Code Complete cites studies where routines up to 100–200 lines show no defect penalty; cohesion matters more than length.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.text: McConnell's comment kinds, worst to best: {{c1::repeat of the code}} (delete), {{c2::explanation of the code}} (fix the code instead), marker (TODO), {{c3::summary}}, {{c4::description of intent}}, and information that cannot be expressed in code (references, licences).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Why does Google's style philosophy favour consistency over local optimality?
notes.back: Code is read far more than written, and consistency scales: tooling works, engineers move between projects, and rules that 'pull their weight' remove debate.
notes.extra: Readability: a per-language certification that an engineer writes idiomatic, consistent code; granted via review.
notes.source: Winters et al. · SWE at Google

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::03 Naming, Comments & Readability
notes.front: Ousterhout on conventions: why not change an existing convention even if yours is better?
notes.back: Consistency's value is that readers can rely on it without thinking. A better rule applied to half the code is worse than a mediocre rule applied everywhere.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Beck's two hats?
notes.back: Adding function and refactoring are different activities. Wear one hat at a time and swap consciously; never do both in the same step.
notes.analogy: A chef either cooks or cleans the station; stirring with one hand and scrubbing with the other spoils both.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Refactoring vs rewriting: how do you decide?
notes.back: Refactor when the code mostly works and you can test it. Rewrite when it is so broken that repair costs more than starting over. Rewrites also lose the team's theory of the system.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: The Rule of Three?
notes.back: First time, just do it. Second time, wince but duplicate. Third time, refactor to remove the duplication.
notes.analogy: Once is chance, twice is coincidence, three times is a pattern worth a name.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: What is preparatory refactoring?
notes.back: Refactor first so the feature becomes easy to add: make the change easy, then make the easy change.
notes.analogy: Clearing the workbench before the repair, not during it.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Fowler's Design Stamina Hypothesis?
notes.back: Good internal design lets you keep adding features quickly; poor design slows you until you crawl. The payback period is weeks, not years.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Divergent Change vs Shotgun Surgery: how to tell apart?
notes.back: Divergent Change: one module changes for many different reasons. Shotgun Surgery: one reason forces changes in many modules. Duals of 'one change, one place'.
notes.analogy: One drawer holding tax forms, socks and tools (divergent) vs your address copied into twenty forms (shotgun).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.text: Code smells: a method more interested in another class's data is {{c1::Feature Envy}}; using string/int for domain concepts is {{c2::Primitive Obsession}}; hooks for a future that never comes is {{c3::Speculative Generality}}; a comment explaining bad code is {{c4::a deodorant}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Feathers' definition of legacy code, and why that definition?
notes.back: Code without tests. Without tests you can't tell whether a change improved or degraded it, however new or well written.
notes.source: Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: The Legacy Code Dilemma?
notes.back: To change code safely we need tests; to get tests in place we usually have to change code. Resolution: minimal, conservative dependency-breaking edits done without tests.
notes.source: Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: What is a seam?
notes.back: A place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place. Every seam has an enabling point where you choose the behaviour.
notes.analogy: A seam in cloth: the garment comes apart there without cutting fabric.
notes.source: Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Object seam vs link seam: difference?
notes.back: Object seam: subclass and override a method, chosen at the call site. Link seam: swap a library or module at link/import time. Object seams are the object-oriented (OO) workhorse.
notes.source: Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Feathers: the two reasons to break a dependency?
notes.back: Sensing: to observe effects you otherwise couldn't. Separation: to get the code into a test harness at all.
notes.source: Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: How does Feathers write a characterization test when nobody knows the behaviour?
notes.back: Assert a value you know is wrong, run, paste the actual result into the assertion. The test now pins current behaviour, bugs included.
notes.extra: Pitfall: fix a pinned bug only if nobody depends on it (Hyrum's Law).
notes.source: Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: What is a tidying?
notes.back: A small, safe, structure-only change: guard clause, dead code removal, explaining variable, reading order, extract helper. A subset of refactoring you can do in minutes.
notes.analogy: "Tidyings are the Pringles of software design": once you start, you can't stop at one.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Why keep structure changes and behaviour changes in separate commits?
notes.back: Structure changes are reversible and need little review; behaviour changes are not. Mixing them makes both harder to verify and to revert.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.text: Tidy First? options: {{c1::tidy first}} when it makes the change easier now; {{c2::tidy after}} when you'll return soon; {{c3::tidy later}} as a listed long-term investment; {{c4::never}} for code you won't touch again.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Beck's empirical definition of coupling?
notes.back: A and B are coupled with respect to change Δ if changing A for Δ requires changing B. Coupling is defined by changes, not by call graphs.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Cohesion vs coupling: what is the relationship?
notes.back: Coupling: elements that must change together. Cohesion: putting such co-changing elements in the same unit. Cohesion is coupling kept inside one boundary.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Constantine's Equivalence?
notes.back: cost(software) ≈ cost(change) ≈ cost(big changes) ≈ coupling. A few huge changes dominate cost, and they are huge because changes ripple across coupled elements.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Beck: software's two kinds of value, and what design buys?
notes.back: Cash flows from today's behaviour, and options on future behaviour. Design increases option value; it matters most in volatile environments.
notes.analogy: A convertible lease: you pay a little now for the right to change your mind later.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Tactical vs strategic programming: difference?
notes.back: Tactical: ship the feature now, each shortcut adds complexity. Strategic: the main goal is a great design that also works; invest 10–20% continuously.
notes.extra: Tactical tornado: the prolific coder who leaves wreckage others must clean up.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Hyrum's Law?
notes.back: With enough users of an API, it does not matter what the contract promises: every observable behaviour will be depended on by somebody.
notes.analogy: Leave a side door unlocked long enough and the delivery drivers will treat it as the entrance.
notes.extra: Examples: hash ordering, timing, error-message text all become contracts.
notes.source: Winters et al. · SWE at Google

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Google: 'software engineering is programming integrated over time'. What changes with time?
notes.back: Code that lives long must survive upgrades, dependency churn and Hyrum's Law. The question 'how long will this live?' decides how much engineering it deserves.
notes.source: Winters et al. · SWE at Google

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: Don't repeat yourself (DRY) vs the wrong abstraction: when is duplication the better choice?
notes.back: When the shared code would need flags and special cases for each caller. Duplication is far cheaper than an abstraction that bends to fit; inline it and let it diverge.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::04 Code Evolution: Refactoring, Tidying & Legacy
notes.front: How do you make a large change on trunk without a long-lived branch?
notes.back: Branch by abstraction: put an abstraction over the old implementation, build the new one behind it, switch, then delete the old. Trunk stays green throughout.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: What is a design pattern, and why is the name the most valuable part?
notes.back: A named problem–solution pair with its consequences. The name lets a team discuss a design at a higher level than classes and methods.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Gang of Four (GoF): why program to an interface, not an implementation?
notes.back: Clients that know only the interface can be given any implementation, now or later. Binding to a concrete class fixes the choice at compile time.
notes.analogy: Any brand of bulb fits a standard socket; the lamp never knows which one.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Gang of Four (GoF): why favour composition over inheritance?
notes.back: Inheritance is white-box reuse: subclasses see parent internals and are fixed at compile time. Composition is black-box, swappable at run time, and keeps each class focused.
notes.analogy: Lego bricks (composition) vs a mould you must recast to change (inheritance).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.text: Gang of Four (GoF) catalogue by what varies: algorithm → {{c1::Strategy}}; object creation → {{c2::Factory / Builder}}; incompatible interface → {{c3::Adapter}}; responsibilities without subclassing → {{c4::Decorator}}; part–whole trees → {{c5::Composite}}; a request as an object → {{c6::Command}}.
notes.extra: Meta-principle: encapsulate the concept that varies.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: The Hollywood Principle, and what it distinguishes?
notes.back: "Don't call us, we'll call you": a framework calls your code (inversion of control). A library is code you call; a framework calls you.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Adapter vs Facade vs Proxy: how to tell?
notes.back: Adapter converts one interface into the one a client expects. Facade offers a simpler interface to a subsystem. Proxy keeps the same interface and controls access.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Why is Decorator both the showcase and the cautionary tale?
notes.back: It adds responsibilities at run time without subclass explosion, but stacked decorators (Java input/output (I/O) streams) give many shallow classes a user must assemble.
notes.source: GoF · Design Patterns · Ousterhout · Philosophy of Software Design

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Norvig's critique: what happens to Gang of Four (GoF) patterns in dynamic languages?
notes.back: 16 of 23 become invisible or trivial: first-class functions replace Strategy, Command and Template Method; multimethods replace Visitor. Patterns mark missing language features.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: The counter-argument to 'patterns are just missing features'?
notes.back: Some patterns describe structure in the problem, not the language: Composite, Observer, Adapter, Facade stay useful. And the shared vocabulary survives even when the code is a lambda.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.text: Modern equivalents: Strategy → {{c1::a lambda}}; Iterator → {{c2::generators / for-each}}; Observer → {{c3::events or reactive streams}}; Visitor → {{c4::pattern matching on sum types}}; Singleton → {{c5::a dependency injection (DI) container}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Why is Singleton the most criticised pattern?
notes.back: It is a global in disguise: hidden shared state, hidden dependencies, and no way to substitute it in tests. Feathers calls it the enemy of testing.
notes.source: GoF · Design Patterns · Feathers · Working Effectively with Legacy Code

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Transaction Script vs Domain Model: when does each win?
notes.back: Transaction Script (one procedure per request) is cheaper for simple logic. Domain Model costs more up front but its effort curve stays flat as rules grow.
notes.extra: Catch: you cannot measure where on the complexity curve you are; the crossover is a judgement.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Active Record vs Data Mapper?
notes.back: Active Record: the object wraps a row and carries its own persistence (Rails). Data Mapper: a separate layer moves data so domain objects stay ignorant of the database (Hibernate).
notes.analogy: Active Record: the letter carries its own stamp and address. Data Mapper: a mailroom addresses and sends letters that know nothing about post.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.text: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA) object-relational behaviours: track all changes in a business transaction and commit once → {{c1::Unit of Work}}; one in-memory object per row → {{c2::Identity Map}}; load related data only when touched → {{c3::Lazy Load}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: Fowler's First Law of Distributed Object Design?
notes.back: Don't distribute your objects. Remote calls are orders of magnitude slower, so cross boundaries only with coarse-grained Remote Facades and data transfer objects (DTOs).
notes.extra: The lineage behind 'microservices are not distributed objects' and monolith-first.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: The Dependency Rule of Clean Architecture?
notes.back: Source-code dependencies point only inward, toward higher-level policy. Nothing in an inner ring may name anything in an outer ring.
notes.analogy: An onion: the inner layers do not know the skin exists.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: How does the Dependency Inversion Principle let control flow outward while dependencies point inward?
notes.back: The inner ring owns an interface; the outer ring implements it. The call crosses the boundary outward, but the source dependency points inward.
notes.extra: Older name: Fowler's Separated Interface in Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA) — interface in one package, implementation in another.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::05 Design Patterns & Their Critics
notes.front: The main critique of Clean Architecture as practised?
notes.back: Heavy layering and data transfer object (DTO) mapping for create, read, update, delete (CRUD) systems; Accelerate found loose coupling predicts performance, not any particular onion; and 'the database is a detail' ignores that data outlives applications.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.text: McIlroy's Unix philosophy: write programs that {{c1::do one thing and do it well}}; write programs to {{c2::work together}}; write programs to handle {{c3::text streams}}, because that is a universal interface.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Why did Unix bet on text streams as the universal interface?
notes.back: Every tool can read, write, inspect and debug text with no shared library or schema, so programs written years apart still compose.
notes.analogy: Paper forms any clerk can read vs a proprietary filing cabinet only one vendor can open.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Text pipeline vs object pipeline: what did PowerShell and JSON change?
notes.back: Text forces every consumer to re-parse; typed objects keep structure but need a shared runtime. The trade is universality vs. losing re-parsing bugs.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Rule of Separation: policy from mechanism?
notes.back: Mechanisms (how) change slowly; policies (what to do) change fast. Keep them apart so policy can change without touching the engine. X Window supplies mechanism, no policy.
notes.analogy: A thermostat is the mechanism; the schedule you set on it is the policy.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Rule of Representation?
notes.back: Fold knowledge into data so the program logic can be stupid and robust. Data is easier to inspect and change than control flow.
notes.extra: Echo: Pike's 'data dominates'; Brooks' 'show me your tables and I won't need your flowcharts'.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Rule of Least Surprise?
notes.back: Do the least surprising thing: reuse conventions users already know, in interfaces, flags and formats. Novelty is a cost the user pays.
notes.analogy: Light switches go up for on; a house that inverts it makes every guest fumble.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Rules of Silence and Repair: how do they fit together?
notes.back: Silence: when there is nothing surprising to say, say nothing. Repair: when you must fail, fail noisily and as early as possible. Quiet success, loud failure.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Why does Raymond call robustness the child of transparency and simplicity?
notes.back: A program whose workings you can see and whose state space is small is one you can reason about, debug and trust under odd inputs.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.text: Pike's rules: you can't tell where a program spends its time, so {{c1::measure}}; fancy algorithms are slow when {{c2::n is small}}, and n is usually small; fancy algorithms are {{c3::buggier}}; {{c4::data dominates}}: choose the right structures and the algorithms are obvious.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Transparency vs discoverability?
notes.back: Transparency: you can see how it works. Discoverability: you can find out what it does and how to use it. A program can have either without the other.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Why does Raymond say the big win of a minilanguage is 'shifting the level'?
notes.back: A notation fitted to the domain (regex, make, awk) says in one line what takes pages of general code, and is checkable by the domain's own rules.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Unix's preference for many cooperating processes over one complex process: what is its modern descendant, and what carries over?
notes.back: Microservices and sidecars. Both inherit the strengths (isolation, independent replacement) and the costs (coordination, serialisation, debugging across boundaries).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Cathedral vs Bazaar: what distinguishes the two development styles?
notes.back: Cathedral: a small group builds carefully in private and releases rarely. Bazaar: develop in the open, release early and often, treat users as co-developers.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Linus's Law, and why it holds?
notes.back: "Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow." Debugging parallelises: each tester brings a different mental model, and finding a bug needs little coordination.
notes.analogy: Twenty proofreaders each catch different typos; no coordination needed, just the one editor who collects them.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::06 Unix Philosophy & Composition
notes.front: Why doesn't Brooks' Law sink the bazaar?
notes.back: Brooks assumed every pair must communicate. In a bazaar, testers talk to the maintainer, not each other (many-to-one), so communication cost grows linearly.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Dijkstra's core argument against goto?
notes.back: Keep the gap between the static program text and the dynamic process small. With structured constructs, a few textual indices tell you where the process is.
notes.analogy: A book with page numbers vs one you can only read by following 'see page X' arrows.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Dijkstra on testing?
notes.back: Testing shows the presence of bugs, never their absence. Only reasoning about the program can give confidence beyond the cases tried.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: The end-to-end argument: what is the careful file transfer example?
notes.back: Even with reliable links, bytes can corrupt in disks, buffers or software at either end. Only an end-to-end check by the application can confirm the file arrived.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: End-to-end argument: when is a lower-layer version of a function still justified?
notes.back: Only as a performance optimisation (e.g. link-level retransmission on a lossy link). It can never replace the end-to-end check for correctness.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Nygard: why is every integration point a crack starter?
notes.back: Every socket, database (DB) and remote call can hang, refuse or lie, and failure propagates along coupling. 'Every integration point will eventually fail.'
notes.analogy: Cracks in a hull run along the welds: the joints are where stress concentrates.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Nygard: what is the lesson of the airline check-in outage?
notes.back: One uncaught SQLException in pool checkout blocked threads, which cascaded to callers and took check-in down for hours. Failure modes must be designed, not left to chance.
notes.extra: Framing: 'feature complete' is not 'production ready'; the system spends its life in operation.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Impulse vs stress in Nygard's stability vocabulary?
notes.back: Impulse: a sudden shock (a flash crowd, a deep link in a marketing email). Stress: sustained pressure (slow dependency, leaking memory). Stable systems survive both.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Why does Nygard call a slow response worse than a refusal?
notes.back: A refusal frees the caller at once. A slow response ties up the caller's threads and pools, so the slowness spreads upstream. Prefer failing fast.
notes.analogy: A waiter who never comes back is worse than one who says 'we're out of that'.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Nygard's Steady State pattern?
notes.back: For every mechanism that accumulates a resource (logs, rows, cache entries), build another that recycles it. Systems needing human 'fiddling' don't stay up.
notes.analogy: A bathtub with the tap running needs the drain open, or it overflows eventually.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Nygard's Force Multiplier antipattern and Governor pattern?
notes.back: Automation amplifies mistakes (an autoscaler removing every 'unhealthy' node). A governor slows automation when it acts destructively, so humans can intervene.
notes.analogy: A steam-engine governor caps speed before the boiler bursts.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Nygard: 'hope is not a design method'. What does it demand?
notes.back: Decide in advance how each component fails, what it does when a dependency fails, and test those modes, instead of assuming the happy path.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Slips vs mistakes (Norman)?
notes.back: Slip: right goal, wrong action (typo, wrong button, mode error). Mistake: wrong goal from a faulty model or rule. Different cures: slips need better signifiers, mistakes need better conceptual models.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: What is a mode error, and what is its API analogue?
notes.back: The same action means different things depending on hidden state. In tooling: kubectl acting on the wrong context, git checkout doing two unrelated jobs.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Forcing functions applied to API design?
notes.back: Make the wrong action impossible: types that make illegal states unrepresentable (interlock), required confirmation for destructive calls (lock-in), no delete without an id (lock-out).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Gulf of Execution vs Gulf of Evaluation?
notes.back: Execution: 'how do I do it?' (bridged by discoverable names, docs, autocomplete). Evaluation: 'what happened?' (bridged by feedback, errors that say what, why, what next).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Affordance vs signifier, for an API?
notes.back: Affordance: what the thing allows (a method can be called). Signifier: the cue that communicates it (name, types, docs). A boolean flag parameter affords but barely signifies.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Norman's three models: why can a designer only communicate through the system image?
notes.back: The designer's model lives in their head; the user builds their own from what the artefact shows. For an API the system image is names, types, docs and observed behaviour.
notes.extra: Hyrum's Law is what happens when the system image leaks the implementation.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: Assertions vs error handling (McConnell)?
notes.back: Assertions: for conditions that should never happen; they document assumptions and fail loudly in development. Error handling: for conditions that will happen; it recovers.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::07 Correctness, Errors & Robustness in Production
notes.front: McConnell's barricade?
notes.back: Validate and sanitise data at the boundary; treat everything inside as trusted. The operating room is sterile because the waiting room is not.
notes.analogy: Hospital: scrub at the door, not at every bed.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Why is the man-month a myth?
notes.back: People and months trade only for partitionable tasks with no communication. Software has sequential constraints and communication needs, so adding people adds overhead.
notes.analogy: Nine women cannot bear a child in one month.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Brooks' Law vs Amdahl-style parallelism: how do they differ?
notes.back: Amdahl: the serial fraction caps speedup, but more workers never hurt. Brooks: training plus n(n−1)/2 communication paths make more workers actively slow a late project.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: The second-system effect, and its antidote?
notes.back: A designer's second system is the most dangerous: all ideas held back from the first get added. Antidote: discipline, and a byte/microsecond budget for every feature.
notes.analogy: The second album stuffed with every idea the label cut from the first.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Why does Brooks rank conceptual integrity above everything in system design?
notes.back: A system expressing one coherent set of ideas is easier to learn and use than one with many uncoordinated good ideas. Reims cathedral vs a patchwork.
notes.analogy: Reims cathedral: one design followed for generations beats many brilliant additions.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: 'Plan to throw one away': what did Brooks later say about it?
notes.back: He retracted it in 1995: the waterfall assumption behind it was wrong. Grow software incrementally instead of building one version to discard.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.text: Theory of Constraints, five focusing steps: {{c1::identify}} the constraint; {{c2::exploit}} it (never let it idle); {{c3::subordinate}} everything else to it; {{c4::elevate}} it (add capacity); if it moves, {{c5::start again}} and don't let inertia become the constraint.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Herbie on the hike: what does the story teach?
notes.back: The slowest hiker sets the troop's pace. Dependent events plus statistical fluctuation mean variance accumulates downstream; put Herbie in front and lighten his pack.
notes.analogy: A convoy moves at the speed of its slowest truck, and gaps only grow.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Drum–Buffer–Rope?
notes.back: The constraint beats the drum (sets the pace); a buffer in front of it absorbs upstream variance; a rope releases new work only at the constraint's rate.
notes.analogy: A conveyor belt paced by its slowest station, with a small pile in front of it and no new parts loaded faster than it can eat.
notes.extra: Modern form: the rope is a work in progress (WIP) limit; the buffer is a small ready-queue before the bottleneck team.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.text: Phoenix Project's four types of work: {{c1::business projects}}, {{c2::internal IT projects}}, {{c3::changes}}, and {{c4::unplanned work}}, the 'silent killer' that displaces the other three.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Brent as the constraint: what is the fix?
notes.back: Protect him: stop routing escalations to him, document and standardise his knowledge so others can do the work. The knowledge in his head is the bottleneck.
notes.extra: Naur's point: the theory of the system is in one person's head.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Phoenix Project's wait-time formula?
notes.back: Wait time ∝ % busy / % idle. At 50% utilisation a task waits 1 unit; at 90%, 9; at 99%, 99. High utilisation destroys flow.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Which of the Three Ways do blameless post-mortems and fault injection belong to, and why?
notes.back: The Third Way (continual learning). Both treat failure as a source of practice and knowledge, building mastery through repetition.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Continuous Delivery's opening one-line-change question?
notes.back: "How long would it take to deploy a change of one line, and can you do it repeatably and reliably?" It measures cycle time and process health at once.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: 'If it hurts, do it more often': why does it work?
notes.back: Painful activities (integration, deployment, testing) hurt because they are rare and big. Doing them constantly forces automation and shrinks each step.
notes.analogy: Stretching daily hurts less than once a year.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Why build the binary once and promote the same artefact?
notes.back: Rebuilding per environment risks differences in compiler, dependencies or flags. Promoting one artefact means what you tested is what you ship; only configuration varies.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.text: Deployment pipeline stages: {{c1::commit stage}} (under ten minutes: compile, unit tests, analysis) → {{c2::automated acceptance tests}} → {{c3::capacity tests}} → {{c4::manual / exploratory / user acceptance testing (UAT)}} → {{c5::release}}. Confidence rises and cost rises; fail fast in the cheap stages.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.text: Accelerate's four key metrics: tempo = {{c1::lead time for changes}} (commit to production) and {{c2::deployment frequency}}; stability = {{c3::mean time to restore}} and {{c4::change failure rate}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: What did Accelerate find about the speed vs stability trade-off?
notes.back: There isn't one. High performers excel at both; the practices that make deployment frequent also make failures small and quick to restore.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Why does Accelerate reject velocity, utilisation and lines of code as metrics?
notes.back: They measure local output, not global outcomes, and are gamed. Good metrics are system-level, outcome-based and hard to improve by hurting another team.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Lead time vs cycle time?
notes.back: Lead time: from request (or commit, in Accelerate) to running in production, including waiting. Cycle time: from work actively started to done. Lead time ≥ cycle time.
notes.analogy: Restaurant: lead time runs from ordering to eating; cycle time from the chef starting to plating.
notes.source: Forsgren, Humble & Kim · Accelerate · Humble & Farley · Continuous Delivery

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: Accelerate's main architecture finding?
notes.back: Loosely coupled architecture, where teams test and deploy on demand without coordinating with others, is the biggest technical predictor. System type matters far less than testability and deployability.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.front: What did Accelerate find about external change approval boards?
notes.back: No correlation with stability and a negative one with speed. Peer review inside the team works as well for stability and far better for tempo.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::08 Flow & Delivery: Brooks to Accelerate
notes.text: Westrum's test, applied by Accelerate: in a {{c1::pathological}} culture messengers are shot; in a {{c2::bureaucratic}} one they are neglected; in a {{c3::generative}} one they are trained and failure leads to inquiry.
notes.extra: How culture changes: by changing practices, not by posters (echoing Peopleware).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Bentley's bit-vector sort: what made it possible?
notes.back: Asking the right questions first: ten million distinct 7-digit numbers, ~1 MB. One bit per possible number fits, and the sort becomes trivial.
notes.analogy: A pigeonhole wall: drop each letter in its numbered slot and read the wall left to right.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Cracking the oyster: what is the first step of any programming problem?
notes.back: Define the problem carefully. Most of the work was in pinning down what the user actually needed; the right problem is half the solution.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Why does Bentley insist on a back-of-the-envelope estimate before building?
notes.back: A quick estimate with safety factors tells you whether the design can work at all, before you spend a week finding out. Estimate, then measure.
notes.extra: Mnemonic: π seconds is a nanocentury; the Rule of 72 for doubling times.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: What does Bentley's binary search story show?
notes.back: Published 1946, first correct version 1962; in his classes only ~10% of professionals got it right. Simple code needs invariants and proof, not confidence.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: What is a loop invariant for?
notes.back: It states what the loop maintains every iteration, so you can argue the loop is correct and know what is true when it exits. Write it before the body.
notes.analogy: A ledger that must balance after every single entry: check it each step and the year-end balances itself.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.text: Bentley's aha algorithms: rotate a vector in place with {{c1::three reversals}} (reverse A, reverse B, reverse the whole); find anagrams by {{c2::signing each word with its sorted letters, then sorting}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP): procedure vs process?
notes.back: A recursive procedure (calls itself) can generate an iterative process if state lives in the arguments (tail recursion). Shape of execution ≠ shape of text.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)'s sequences as conventional interfaces: what idea is it?
notes.back: Express computations as enumerate → map → filter → accumulate over a stream of elements, so stages compose like signal-processing blocks.
notes.extra: Ancestor of language integrated query (LINQ), Java Streams and data pipelines.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Stratified design in the picture language of Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)?
notes.back: Each layer is a complete language for building the next: primitives, combination, abstraction, again and again. Change one layer without rewriting the rest.
notes.analogy: Alphabet → words → sentences → stories, each level with its own grammar.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Extreme programming (XP)'s core bet on the cost-of-change curve?
notes.back: Change need not get exponentially dearer over time if tests, refactoring and integration keep it cheap. 'Embrace change' is only rational if that holds.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Extreme programming (XP): of cost, time, quality and scope, which is negotiable?
notes.back: Only scope. Cutting quality slows you down rather than saving time; cost and time are usually fixed from outside.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Why is you aren't gonna need it (YAGNI) only safe together with refactoring?
notes.back: Building for today's need is a bet that you can change the design later. Without cheap refactoring the bet fails and 'simplest thing' becomes a dead end.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests (GOOS): why build the walking skeleton before any real feature?
notes.back: The first feature is the hardest: it forces build, deploy and end-to-end test infrastructure into existence. Everything after rides on that pipeline.
notes.analogy: Lay the track end to end and run one empty carriage before building the dining car.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests (GOOS): 'listen to the tests', what does a hard-to-write test tell you?
notes.back: A design smell: too many dependencies (does too much), too many expectations (confused responsibilities), bloated constructors. Fix the object, not the test.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Values vs objects in Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests (GOOS)?
notes.back: Values: immutable, no identity, compared by content (money, dates). Objects: identity, state and behaviour; they are the communicating parts of the system.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.text: Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests (GOOS) object peer stereotypes: {{c1::dependencies}} (required, passed in the constructor), {{c2::notifications}} (fire-and-forget observers), {{c3::adjustments}} (policies that tweak behaviour).

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Petzold: why is the relay the component that makes a computer possible?
notes.back: It is a switch controlled by a signal, so one circuit can control another. From that you build gates, from gates an adder, and so on up the stack.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Petzold: what does feedback between two gates add?
notes.back: Memory. A pair of cross-coupled not-or (NOR) gates (a latch) holds a bit after the input is removed; from latches come registers and RAM.
notes.analogy: Two people each saying 'I'll stay if you stay': the agreement persists after the question stops.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: Why does McConnell call design a wicked problem?
notes.back: You must solve it once to understand it: the Tacoma Narrows oscillation was only visible after the bridge was built. Design is heuristic and iterative by nature.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::09 Programming Craft & Problem Solving
notes.front: McConnell's defect-cost increase?
notes.back: Fixing a defect costs 10–100× more the later it is found. So define the problem, requirements and architecture before construction, scaled to the project.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Kent's central thesis about data models?
notes.back: We are not modelling reality, but the way people process information about reality. A database is a model of a shared mental model, never of the world.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Kent's oneness problem: what is 'one book'?
notes.back: A physical copy, an edition, the work, or a set of volumes? Deciding what counts as one thing is a modelling decision, not an observation.
notes.analogy: Is a daily flight 'the same flight' tomorrow? Only if your model says so.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Why do surrogate keys exist, in Kent's terms?
notes.back: Natural identity is unstable: people change names, companies reorganise, parts get renumbered. A meaningless key records our decision that it is still 'the same' thing.
notes.analogy: A passport number keeps identifying you after you change your name, job and address.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Kent on categories: the plastic letter that is 'N' or 'Z'?
notes.back: Type can depend on orientation, use or context, not intrinsic form. The same entity is employee, customer and shareholder: roles, not fixed types.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: What is a name, according to Kent?
notes.back: A relationship between a symbol and a thing in a context. Names are unique only within a scope (a part number per supplier), and one thing may have many.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Kent: is 'colour' an attribute of the car or a relationship to a Colour entity?
notes.back: Either; it is a modelling choice. An attribute is a relationship we chose not to model as a thing, and the business will later disagree with the choice.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.text: Kent's many meanings of null: {{c1::unknown}}, {{c2::not applicable}}, {{c3::not yet determined}}, and refused or withheld. One symbol, several facts, which is why nulls breed bugs.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: How does Kent's work anticipate bounded contexts?
notes.back: Ambiguity is inherent, so build a model good enough for a purpose with explicit boundaries. 'Customer' means different things in different departments: scope it, don't unify it.
notes.extra: The domain-driven design (DDD) deck covers bounded context mechanics; this is the epistemology behind it.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP): what is data?
notes.back: Whatever satisfies the contract of its operations: if (car (cons x y)) is x, pairs exist, even when cons is implemented as a closure.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP): what does assignment cost you?
notes.back: It introduces time: the same expression can mean different things at different moments, 'sameness' becomes a question, and the substitution model stops working.
notes.analogy: A photograph vs a live camera feed: only one looks the same every time you check.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Objects vs streams as two views of change in Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)?
notes.back: Object view: the world is things with state that changes. Stream view: the world is signals over time; state is a stream of values and no assignment is needed.
notes.extra: Ancestor of functional reactive programming and event sourcing.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)'s data-directed programming: what problem does the operation table solve?
notes.back: Adding a new type or a new operation without editing existing code (additivity). A table indexed by (operation, type) replaces switch statements.
notes.extra: The same tension later named the expression problem.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Meadows: why infer a system's purpose from its behaviour, not its stated goals?
notes.back: The purpose of a system is what it does. If a process that claims to value quality consistently ships defects, defect-shipping is its real purpose.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Delivery as stocks and flows: what are work in progress (WIP), started work and deployed work?
notes.back: WIP is a stock; starting and deploying are the inflow and outflow. The stock changes only through its flows, so lead time falls by limiting inflow or raising outflow.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::10 Data, Models & Reality
notes.front: Meadows' bounded rationality: why do reasonable actors produce bad system outcomes?
notes.back: Each acts sensibly on the information it has, which is local and delayed. Fix the information flows and incentives, not the people.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Peopleware's central claim?
notes.back: The major problems of our work are sociological, not technological. Managers get leverage from the human side, not from tools.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Peopleware on flow: why do interruptions cost more than their duration?
notes.back: Entering flow takes ~15 minutes; each interruption resets the clock. Measure uninterrupted hours (the E-factor), not hours present.
notes.analogy: A diver surfacing for every phone call never reaches depth.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: What did the Coding War Games find?
notes.back: 10:1 spread between individuals, but the best cluster in the same organisations; performance tracked quiet, private workspace, not language, experience or salary.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.text: Peopleware's teamicide: {{c1::defensive management}}, {{c2::bureaucracy}}, {{c3::physical separation}}, {{c4::fragmentation of time}}, quality reduction, phony deadlines, clique control, and (3rd ed.) overtime and internal competition.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Why can't you make a team jell?
notes.back: Jelling is emergent; management can only remove teamicide and give the team a real challenge. Signs: low turnover, identity, joint ownership, enjoyment.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Spanish vs English theory of value?
notes.back: Spanish: value is fixed, extract more via unpaid overtime. English: value is created through productivity. Overtime is Spanish and is followed by undertime.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Why does 'Big-M Methodology' backfire?
notes.back: It produces malicious compliance, paperwork and the absence of responsibility. Prefer convergence of method: shared practice that people adopt because it helps.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Hamming: why do most researchers never do important work?
notes.back: They don't work on important problems, and they don't have the courage to try. Ask: what are the important problems in my field, and why aren't I working on them?

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Hamming's open door?
notes.back: Those with the door open are interrupted more but know what matters; those with it closed work harder on the wrong problems. Stay connected to the field.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Hamming's compound interest of effort?
notes.back: Knowledge and productivity compound: a little more effort, applied consistently, yields far more over a career. Luck favours the prepared mind.
notes.analogy: Two savers at 5% and 6% end a career tens of percent apart.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Conway's original claim, and the mechanism behind it?
notes.back: A system's structure copies the communication structure of its organisation, because designers can only agree interfaces along lines where they talk.
notes.analogy: A building planned by three firms that never meet gets three staircases that do not join up.
notes.extra: His example: four groups building a compiler produce a four-pass compiler. Team Topologies covers the inverse manoeuvre.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Why does Conway say a large organisation's design space is constrained before design starts?
notes.back: The org chart fixes who can communicate, so alternatives that need other interfaces are never considered. Choose the organisation with the design in mind.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Brooks' surgical team: what problem does it solve?
notes.back: Conceptual integrity with throughput: one chief programmer designs and codes, supported by specialists. A 200-person project with 20 minds doing design.
notes.analogy: An operating theatre: one surgeon cuts; the team amplifies, never second-guesses.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.text: Google's team culture pillars (HRT): {{c1::humility}} (you are not the centre of the universe), {{c2::respect}} (care about colleagues as people), {{c3::trust}} (believe they are competent and let them drive).
notes.extra: HRT stands for humility, respect, trust.
notes.source: Winters et al. · SWE at Google

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Graham's Blub paradox?
notes.back: A programmer of language Blub sees less powerful languages as lacking, but more powerful ones as 'weird'; power you don't have you can't recognise.
notes.analogy: Flatlanders dismiss the third dimension as a trick while pitying the one-dimensional.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Graham's bottom-up design?
notes.back: Don't only decompose the problem downward; build the language upward toward it with domain-specific helpers, until the program is short in the new vocabulary.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Naur: programming as theory building. Why do hand-overs and rewrites fail?
notes.back: The program is the theory in the developers' heads; the text is a partial record. Documentation can't transfer the theory, so continuity of people is what preserves a system.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::11 People, Teams & Craft
notes.front: Extreme programming (XP)'s energised work rule?
notes.back: Work only as many hours as you can sustain productively (the 40-hour week). Overtime is a symptom of a planning problem, not a cure.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Parnas 1972, On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules: modularise around {{c1::design decisions likely to change}}, not processing steps; worked example: {{c2::the KWIC index}}.
notes.extra: KWIC stands for key word in context.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Brooks 1986, No Silver Bullet: software difficulty is mostly {{c1::essential}} (complexity, conformity, changeability, invisibility), so no single technique yields {{c2::an order-of-magnitude gain within a decade}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Dijkstra 1968, Go To Statement Considered Harmful: unrestricted jumps destroy the correspondence between {{c1::static program text}} and {{c2::the dynamic process}}; it became the template for every 'X considered harmful'.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Dijkstra 1972, The Humble Programmer: testing shows {{c1::the presence, not the absence, of bugs}}; the competent programmer is aware of {{c2::the limited size of his own skull}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Conway 1968, How Do Committees Invent?: systems copy {{c1::the communication structure of the organisation}} that builds them; example: {{c2::four groups produce a four-pass compiler}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Lampson 1983, Hints for Computer System Design: keep it simple, get it right, make it fast; interfaces should be {{c1::simple, complete, and admit a small fast implementation}}; {{c2::don't generalise}}; use {{c3::hints}} (cheaply checked, possibly wrong) and the end-to-end principle.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Saltzer, Reed & Clark 1984, End-to-End Arguments: a function placed low in the stack is {{c1::redundant or incomplete}}; correctness is checked {{c2::at the endpoints}}; lower-layer help is {{c3::only a performance optimisation}}. Example: careful file transfer.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Hamming 1986, You and Your Research: work on {{c1::important problems}}, keep {{c2::the door open}}, have {{c3::courage}}, and let effort {{c4::compound}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Moseley & Marks 2006, Out of the Tar Pit: complexity comes from {{c1::state and control}}; separate essential from accidental; ideal: {{c2::functional relational programming}}.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Waldo et al. 1994, A Note on Distributed Computing: local/remote transparency fails because of {{c1::latency, memory access, partial failure and concurrency}}; remote objects cannot be treated like local ones.
notes.extra: Distributed-systems mechanics live in the Distributed Systems & Data deck.

notes.deck: Software Engineering Classics::12 Classic Papers in One Line
notes.text: Royce 1970, the 'waterfall' paper: the single-pass diagram is shown {{c1::as a model that is risky and invites failure}}; Royce recommends {{c2::iteration, prototyping ('do it twice') and heavy customer involvement}}. It was later cited as endorsing what it warned against.
